title: The Newcomer Who Is Different
text:
Katherine Phillips, Katie Liljenquist and Margaret Neale studied what happens when a newcomer joins a team. They recruited members of university fraternities and sororities and put them in groups of three from the same house to solve a murder mystery. Each member had some clues, and the group had to decide who the killer was.

After the trio had discussed the case for a while, a fourth person joined. In some groups, the newcomer was from the same fraternity or sorority as the others. In others, the newcomer was from a different house, a socially distinct outsider. The newcomer, like the others, had information and a view about the case.

Groups joined by an outsider were more likely to identify the right suspect than groups joined by an insider. Yet members of those groups found the discussion less pleasant, felt less confident in their decision and believed they had performed worse.

The researchers suggested that the outsider's mere presence made old members think harder: they could not assume agreement, so they examined their own reasoning more carefully and paid more attention to the evidence. The discomfort was part of what improved the result.
lesson: A team that feels comfortable is not always deciding well. Welcome people who are different from the group, and accept some friction as the price of better thinking.
people: Katherine Phillips, Katie Liljenquist, Margaret Neale
source: Phillips, K. W., Liljenquist, K. A., and Neale, M. A. (2009). Is the pain worth the gain? The advantages and liabilities of agreeing with socially distinct newcomers. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 35(3), 336-350.
